founder_profile.founder_motivation: Six years in plant operations watching good companies get fined over paperwork nobody had time to do. I wanted that problem gone.
founder_profile.building_summary: ComplyEdge - compliance reporting software for mid-size Indian manufacturers. Statutory filings that took a team two weeks now take two days.
founder_profile.vision_1_year: Rs 4 Cr ARR and the default compliance tool for mid-size manufacturers in western India.
founder_profile.product_description: Web platform that ingests plant data and auto-generates the statutory environmental and labour compliance reports Indian manufacturers file quarterly.

diagnosis_answers.answer_text: For me, “doing it really well” means being *trusted*—because in compliance, one missed clause can hurt people and kill customer confidence. We already try to be “best” on accuracy (we auto-generate with audit-ready traceability), but the win condition I’m optimizing for is retention: keeping churn at ~3% by getting customers to finish onboarding and actually rely on the platform every month/quarter. If we’re trusted, we’ll naturally grow to Rs 4 cr ARR and become the default tool, but “being first” isn’t the goal—I care whether customers stick and renew.
diagnosis_answers.question_text: When you picture doing this really well, what does 'well' actually mean to you — being first, being the best, or being trusted?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: I decided to build this after I saw a “good” plant get seriously hurt by compliance gaps that were either missed or discovered too late—like audits and documentation slipping by weeks, and the plant taking real downtime/legal pain. After six years running operations, I kept seeing the same pattern: lots of data existed in the plant, but nobody had a reliable system to turn it into ready-to-file compliance reports fast. The tipping point was realizing we could standardize that workflow into software—ingest plant data and auto-generate reports—without depending on a hero auditor, and that it would directly reduce risk and churn (right now it’s ~1.2 Cr ARR and our biggest leak is onboarding/activation, which I haven’t measured tightly enough yet).
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Think back to the moment you decided this was worth actually building, not just thinking about. What tipped it?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Before building, I was just operating plants and relying on “tribal knowledge” to catch compliance gaps—if it wasn’t visible in time, the damage was already done. Now I show up with a builder’s mindset: every week I’m pushing the platform to turn raw plant data into a report automatically, and I’m treating churn like a product bug to debug (we don’t just “sell harder”). I also track onboarding rigorally now—where users drop after signup, what they do in week 1 vs week 4—but I’ll be honest: we still haven’t measured activation time finely enough to know the exact moment people lose confidence.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: What's actually different about how you show up now versus before you started building?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: The last thing I shipped that I wasn’t fully happy with was our “auto-report” export flow—nice on paper, but it was too optimistic about data completeness and we didn’t have enough guardrails for messy plant inputs, so some customers got reports with gaps and had to redo parts. I shipped it anyway because churn was already spiking and sales needed something “new” for onboarding in the next cohort; we were under pressure to prove traction before running out of patience internally. The real issue is I haven’t instrumented the exact drop-off points in that flow (where they abandon vs. where they come back), so I only learned about it from support tickets, not usage data.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last thing you shipped that you weren't fully happy with, but shipped anyway. Why?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: The last win that really felt good was getting 6 manufacturing sites from 3 different customers to start logging data end-to-end and accept the auto-generated compliance report without edits—so the “report in 1 click” promise actually held in the real factory workflow. What made it land was we tightened onboarding around their exact audit cadence (we mapped “what needs evidence when” for Gujarat/MH inspections) and added a pre-check that flags missing documents before the report generation, which cut back-and-forth by ~40% in those accounts. Also, it happened after we fixed a couple of ugly edge cases in the template logic—suddenly the system stopped feeling like it needed us to babysit it.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last win here that actually felt good. What made that one land more than the others?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: The last time I felt completely overwhelmed was ~6 months back when churn spiked and we kept missing renewals—ARR was basically flat at ~₹1 cr while usage was dropping, and we had no clean way to tell *why* customers stopped logging in. I didn’t shut down; I reached out fast and made it very operational: I called every at-risk customer within 48 hours, asked only one thing (“what stopped you from using us weekly?”), and then I forced our team to fix the top 2 blockers in the onboarding flow before adding any new features. It helped, but I’ll be honest—we’re still not measuring the full funnel rigorously (activation vs. first real report vs. “habit” of weekly/monthly logging), so we’re acting from patterns, not yet from hard metrics.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Walk me through the last time you were completely overwhelmed. What did you actually do -- push through, shut down, or reach out?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: I decided it was worth building because I’d seen multiple plants get hurt by compliance gaps that weren’t caught early, and our platform can turn messy plant data into auditable reports automatically—so the customer doesn’t “hope” they’re compliant, they can prove it. Today I still believe it deserves my time, but the sentence has shifted from “we can automate reporting” to “we can materially reduce churn by making onboarding and first value within 14–21 days so they keep using it.”
founder_dna_answers.question_text: If you had to defend why this still deserves your time, in one sentence -- has that sentence changed since you started?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: The one number for me is **net revenue retention (NRR)**—I want it to move from roughly **~85–90% to 95%+** as churn drops. If NRR improves, it means customers aren’t just “logging in once after onboarding,” they’re expanding usage of reports/modules and sticking around long enough for compliance cycles. Churn alone is noisy because we haven’t mapped it to specific onboarding steps/first “successful report generated” events yet, so NRR tells me the real story end-to-end.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: What's the one number that, if it moved, would tell you this is really working?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Last quarter we were tempted to “ship faster” by loosening how our compliance reports map to source evidence—basically auto-filling gaps with assumptions to reduce onboarding time. We did it in one module, and within 3 weeks we saw customer complaints spike (support tickets doubled) because auditors wouldn’t accept the evidence trail, so renewals got shaky and we had to roll back/patch with stricter checks. Growth wanted the friction down; what mattered to me was audit defensibility, so I chose fewer signups in that window over breaking trust.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last time growth tempted you to compromise on something you'd said mattered. What happened?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: The last stretch of work that really gave momentum was when we tightened onboarding: we cut it from ~6 weeks to ~3.5 weeks by forcing a single “data-to-first-report” path and doing live setup calls only when the plant data was complete. That momentum only happened because we finally aligned Engineering + Ops around one measurable output (“first generated compliance report within 7 days of signup”) and we stopped treating onboarding as a training program and started treating it like a conversion funnel. Also, churn had become the existential metric, so leadership stopped letting perfect-but-optional features delay core reliability—our uptime and report generation accuracy stopped being a moving target.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last stretch of work here that gave you real momentum. What conditions made it possible?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Figuring it out as I go
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Thinking about how you're actually building right now -- are you working to a plan you set in advance, or figuring it out as you go?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Last week genuinely got to me because churn was still flat and I saw that most “active” users during onboarding were not converting into report submissions by week 6—so the product wasn’t failing on day one, it was failing in the handoff. I spent 2 full days pulling logs + calling 8 users across Gujarat/Maharashtra to map exactly where they got stuck (data ingestion vs. template setup vs. approvals), then I cut onboarding down from ~6 weeks to a 14-day “first compliance report” sprint with a tighter checklist and daily human follow-ups for the first 10 customers. I didn’t just tweak copy—I replaced one of our intake steps with an in-app guided flow and set a hard internal KPI: 70% of onboarded accounts must generate their first regulatory report within 14 days.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last week here that genuinely got to you. What did you do with it?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: I learned the hard way that “they signed” doesn’t mean “they’ll renew”—we optimized onboarding for features, not for getting the compliance report filed/used end-to-end. First we got wrong the assumption that auto-generated reports alone create value; in reality, customers needed very specific data readiness + a clear workflow inside their plant, and our 6-week onboarding let them stall and churn after a quarter. We don’t have good instrumentation for “where exactly they drop” inside onboarding yet (step-by-step activation/first report submission), so we’ve been guessing a bit, but the biggest mistake was not forcing that success moment by design.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about something you've had to learn the hard way since starting to build. What did you get wrong first?
When something's going wrong, do you want it told to you straight, laid out step by step, or talked through out loud?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Last week I was mid-way through updating our onboarding flow in the product, but I got pulled into a “quick” churn firefight—two accounts had stopped logging in after the 6-week onboarding window. I spent ~2 days digging through logs + support tickets to find the exact drop-off step, and in parallel our junior sales needed an urgent pitch deck refresh for one renewal call. I should’ve put a hard timer + parked the onboarding work, but the immediate revenue risk pulled me into reactive mode.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last time you context-switched mid-task and lost real time to it. What pulled you away?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Right now, I’m still founder-led on sales calls + custom compliance scoping for every mid-size plant, even though we’ve got ~18 people and the product’s supposed to be “default tool.” It’s not scalable because it eats my bandwidth (and the two junior sales folks don’t close fast enough), but I keep doing it because we’re stuck with churn—most accounts sign, use it ~1 quarter, then stop logging in—so I’m trying to prevent bad-fit implementations by getting in early. The uncomfortable part is we haven’t measured onboarding drop-off and time-to-value rigorously yet, so I’m making this call based on gut + anecdotal patterns instead of hard funnels.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: What's the thing you're doing right now that isn't scalable, but you're doing anyway -- and why?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Last month I got pulled into “polishing” the new auto-generation templates for a couple of high-volume laws—cleaning wording, formatting tables, and adding nicer PDFs—without locking the end-to-end workflow with real plant users first. It delayed shipping the updated onboarding checklist and in-app “first report in 30 minutes” flow by ~3 weeks, and churn got worse because new customers still didn’t see a tangible win fast enough. We also still haven’t measured the exact drop-off by step in onboarding, so I’m pretty sure we fixed the wrong thing in the moment.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last time perfectionism cost you real time here. What were you polishing, and what did it delay?

founder_dna_answers.answer_text: Honestly, we haven’t fully measured *why* customers churn after the first quarter—we’re good at tracking “login stopped,” but we don’t have a clean map from onboarding steps → first report generated → sustained usage. We suspect onboarding (the 6-week setup + approvals) is the choke point, but we haven’t instrumented it end-to-end or run cohort comparisons to prove whether it’s time-to-first-compliance-report that kills activation. I also haven’t told anyone internally that our “compliance generated” is happening, but sometimes it’s not the *exact* format/sections plants need for their internal audit cycle, so users don’t feel urgency to keep logging data.
founder_dna_answers.question_text: What's the thing about running this that you haven't told anyone yet?

current_problem_answers.answer_text: Churn. Customers sign up, use the platform for like a quarter, then stop logging in and we don’t retain them—so ARR grows but the logo count slowly bleeds. I suspect onboarding (which takes ~6 weeks) is where we’re losing momentum, but we haven’t measured it cleanly—like time-to-first-report, activation, or why they go quiet. If we can’t confidently fix that “they try it then vanish” loop, nothing else matters.
current_problem_answers.question_text: Now the part that matters most. In your own words, what is the single biggest problem in your business right now? Don't polish it -- say it the way you'd say it to a friend at the end of a long day.

current_problem_answers.answer_text: If my ability to deliver “compliance report → customer confidence → continued usage” broke tomorrow, the business would stop cold. Concretely: churn tied to onboarding + low adoption is killing us, and I haven’t measured the exact drop-off points well enough (I know churn is the issue, but not whether it’s setup, data ingestion quality, report accuracy, or “first successful report” time). If we lost even more onboarding effectiveness—so customers can’t generate their first report in the first ~2 weeks—signups would keep happening but retention would collapse and ARR would flatten fast.
current_problem_answers.question_text: What's the one thing that, if it broke tomorrow, would stop the business cold?

current_problem_answers.answer_text: Last quarter me and my ops lead disagreed on whether to spend the next 4 weeks fixing the report “generation quality” vs tightening onboarding. I pushed for onboarding because we’re losing customers after ~1 quarter (that’s why I’m targeting churn down to 3% in 90 days), and he argued report accuracy is what customers will complain about, not the setup. We ended up compromising—ran a short fix to templates plus added onboarding checklists—but we didn’t measure the causal impact, so both efforts moved slowly and churn didn’t visibly improve. Honestly, we resolved it more by “who has the loudest evidence today” than by a clean experiment—we haven’t instrumented onboarding drop-off tightly enough yet.
current_problem_answers.question_text: Tell me about the last time you and a co-founder or teammate disagreed on what to do next. How was it resolved -- or wasn't it?

current_problem_answers.answer_text: This week I’ve been avoiding the fact that we don’t actually know *why* customers stop using us after ~1 quarter—we’re treating churn like a vague product issue instead of auditing the onboarding funnel. I’ve been side-stepping a painful reset: instrumenting activation (first report generated, first upload cycle completed, time-to-first-value), and then running cohort interviews with the ~10–15 most recent churned accounts to pinpoint the exact drop-off step. Also, I’m avoiding a hard conversation with my sales + onboarding flow—our two junior sellers aren’t closing or qualifying properly, and we’re paying the cost later in 6-week onboarding.
current_problem_answers.question_text: What have you been avoiding this week that you know you need to deal with?

messages.content: In one short sentence: what is 80/20?
The 80/20 rule (Pareto Principle) says roughly 80% of your results come from just 20% of your efforts — so focus on that vital few.
Our churn is 9% monthly and I don't know why.

9% monthly churn is a real red flag — that's roughly two-thirds of a cohort gone within a year if it stays unchecked. But I want to be straight with you: nothing in your diagnosis, memory, or the materials I have access to (which are mostly about your chemical plant production ramp, KPI dashboard, hiring tracker, and sales model) actually covers customer retention or churn drivers. So I can't point to specific data or a diagnosis finding here — I'd just be guessing if I tried to tie it to something in your files.

That said, I can help you think through it properly. A few questions that usually separate the real causes fast:

1. **When does it happen?** Right after signup/first use, or after a few months of usage? Early churn usually = onboarding/expectation mismatch. Later churn usually = value decay, pricing, or a competitor pulling them away.
2. **Who's churning?** Is it concentrated in one segment, plan tier, acquisition channel, or use case? If it's evenly spread, it's likely a core product issue. If it's concentrated, it's more likely a targeting/fit issue.
3. **Have you talked to any of them?** Even 5-10 exit conversations (or a simple exit survey) usually surfaces a dominant reason within the first handful of responses.
4. **Did anything change before the churn spike?** Pricing change, a bad release, support delays, a competitor launch — churn often has a triggering event you can trace back.

If you can pull even rough numbers on when in the lifecycle people drop off, that alone usually points to the fix. Want to dig into any of those threads, or do you have exit/survey data already sitting somewhere we could look at together?
In two short sentences, what is customer churn?

Customer churn is the rate at which customers stop doing business with you over a given period — usually shown as a percentage of customers (or revenue) lost. It's a key health signal: high churn means you're losing customers faster than sustainable growth can offset.

Since you mentioned your churn is 9% monthly — that's quite high (most healthy SaaS/subscription businesses aim for 3-5% or less monthly). Want to dig into possible causes together?
Our monthly churn is 9% and I am not sure why.

That 9% monthly churn is a real number to chase down — it's roughly ~70% of customers gone within a year if it stays flat, so worth digging into now. I don't have any diagnosis or business data on file yet that tells me *why* it's happening for you specifically, so I don't want to guess at a cause. But I can help you think through where to look.

A few questions that usually separate the real culprits:

1. **When do people churn?** Right after signup/onboarding, after first billing cycle, or later after months of use? Early churn usually = onboarding/activation problem. Later churn = value or competitive problem.
2. **Who churns?** Is it concentrated in one segment, plan tier, acquisition channel, or use case? If churn is much higher from one channel (e.g., a paid ads source), that's often an expectations/targeting mismatch, not a product problem.
3. **Have you talked to any churned users directly?** Even 5-10 exit conversations usually surface a dominant pattern (price, missing feature, poor support, found alternative, no longer needed it).
4. **Did anything change around when churn rose?** Pricing change, support quality dip, a competitor's launch, product bug or slowdown?

If you can pull together data like signup cohort curves and even just a rough breakdown by plan/channel, that'll turn "9% and I don't know why" into something diagnosable pretty fast. Want to walk through your funnel step by step together, or do you already have some churn data segmented that we can look at?
In one sentence, what is product-market fit?

Product-market fit is when your product satisfies a real, strong market demand so well that customers actively want it, buy it, and keep coming back — without you having to push hard to convince them.

By the way, that 9% monthly churn you mentioned earlier is worth digging into — if PMF isn't fully locked in, churn is often the clearest signal telling you where the gap is. Want to explore what might be driving it?

ComplyEdge is pitching an auto-compliance tool that turns a 2-week manual reporting job for mid-size Indian manufacturers into a 2-day job, backed by Rs 1.05 Cr ARR and 31 paying plants across Gujarat and Maharashtra. The ask is Rs 8 Cr at a Rs 40 Cr pre-money valuation, to fund sales expansion and entry into South India.

Want me to look at the deck more closely next, like you asked in your other message? I can flag anything that might raise questions from investors.
Read my deck against what you already know about me and my business. Is there anything in it you would push back on before I send this to investors?

Good idea to stress-test this before it goes out. Here's what I'd push back on, just based on the deck itself:

**1. "Best-in-class retention" — no number given.**
Investors will ask for the actual churn or retention rate. Right now this line is a claim, not a fact. If you have the number and it's good, put it in. If you don't have it handy, get it before your first investor call — this is the first thing a diligent investor will poke at.

**2. Rs 40 Cr pre-money on Rs 1.05 Cr ARR — that's a ~38x multiple.**
That's a big multiple for a business with real revenue (versus a pure pre-revenue story). You don't have to lower it, but you should walk in ready to defend it — growth rate, margins, why this space deserves the multiple. If the deck doesn't show growth rate (ARR now vs. 6 or 12 months ago), that's a gap. Add it if the trend is good.

**3. "Repeatable, scalable sales motion" — no proof shown.**
This is a strong claim with nothing backing it in the deck. What's your sales cycle length? Customer acquisition cost? Number of reps and their output? One line of proof here (e.g. "avg sales cycle: X weeks, CAC: Rs Y") would make this claim land instead of sounding like a hope.

**4. South India expansion — no plan detail.**
You're asking for money partly to enter South India, but the deck doesn't say how. Do you already have leads there? Is the compliance regulation the same across states, or does South India have different rules your product needs to handle? If regulation differs by state, that's a real product question investors will ask.

**5. Team section is thin.**
"18 people, founder spent 6 years in plant ops" is good founder-market fit, but investors will want to know who else is on the team — especially anyone senior in tech, sales, or compliance/legal. If you have strong hires, name them.

None of this means the deck is weak — the traction (31 plants, Rs 1.05 Cr ARR, sticky compliance product) is genuinely strong. These are just the spots where a sharp investor will lean in and ask "how do you know that?" — better to have the answer ready, or in the deck, before they ask.

Hey Rohan — let's do this, but I want to be upfront about what I actually have and don't have, so the deck is useful instead of generic.

**What I know about you:**

**What I don't have:**

Here's the thing about churn: it's a strange thing to put front and center in an investor deck. If churn is high, a sharp investor will ask about it either way — so let's decide whether we address it head-on ("here's the problem, here's our plan, here's early proof it's working") or focus the deck on the vision and traction while you handle churn as a live operating issue outside the deck.

To build something real, I need a few numbers from you:
1. How many customers do you have today, and what's your actual churn rate?
2. What's your current ARR (you said above 1 Cr — how much above)?
3. What's your pricing model?
4. Who are you up against — other software, or manual/CA-led processes?
5. What's driving the churn — do you know?

Give me those, and I'll draft a deck structure: problem, product, traction, market, ask. If you'd rather skip straight to a rough draft using placeholders you can fill in later, I can do that too — just say so.
